newsitem.title: MEXICO: Clinton calls for NAFTA to expand across Americas.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for NAFTA to expand across Americas.

text.p: President Bill Clinton called on Wednesday for an expansion of free trade across the Americas, saying the United States' NAFTA partnership with Mexico and Canada had been a big success.

On the third and final day of his visit to Mexico, Clinton told a group of Mexican businessmen that the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) had boosted trade and brought new, well-paid jobs to both nations.
"NAFTA is working for America and it is working for Mexico," Clinton said.
"...we must include more nations in our partnership, so that we can achieve the goal set out at the (1994) Summit of the Americas of a Free Trade Area of the Americas."
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo also sang the praises of free trade, saying Mexico now bought more U.S. exports than Britain and Germany combined.
"We see free trade as one of the most powerful motors of our time for development," Zedillo said, "...for development capable of transforming challenges into opportunities".
Progress toward expanding NAFTA to Chile, the next country in line to join, has so far been held up by opposition in the U.S. Congress. Clinton said he was working to overcome this.
The two presidents also addressed the topics that have dominated the agenda on Clinton's first visit to Mexico -- drugs and illegal immigration.
On both subjects, the U.S. president stressed what has been the abiding theme of his visit -- the need to cooperate, rather than argue, with Mexico.
"Here in Mexico, you must continue your brave fight against illegal drugs," Clinton said. "...Let us resolve to redouble our efforts, not by pointing fingers but by joining hands."

As he has done time and again on the visit, the U.S. leader went out of his way to charm his Mexican audience. He peppered his speech with references to Mexican heroes and reminded the audience of his honeymoon in the Mexican resort of Acapulco nearly 22 years ago.
"Then as now, Me Encanta Mexico (I love Mexico)," Clinton said to loud applause.

Careful as always not to stoke nationalist sentiment in a traditionally anti-American country, Zedillo complimented Clinton on having combined "the legitimate interest of his country with solidarity and respect toward Mexico."
Mexico is the biggest source of narcotics and migrants crossing the 2,000-mile (3,200 km) border into the United States -- a source of considerable irritation to Americans.
For their part, Mexicans are angered by the U.S. demand for drugs that fuels the trade, as well as by what they see as unfair U.S. treatment of Mexican migrants.
Protests, however, have been sparse on Clinton's visit.
Budding demonstrators have complained that the massive police and army presence on the central streets of Mexico's capital has prevented them from even gathering, far less expressing dissent.
With the bulk of Clinton's programme on Wednesday consisting of visits to tourist attractions out of the capital, the main results of the trip came on Tuesday.
Clinton and Zedillo signed an Alliance Against Drugs, pledging their two cabinets would agree a joint strategy against narcotics trafficking, and also signed a declaration on migration.
In his speech on Wednesday, Clinton praised the contribution that Hispanics and Mexican-Americans -- including his Energy Secretary Federico Pena -- had made to the United States.

But he emphasised Washington would not tolerate illegal immigration. "We are a nation of immigrants and of laws," he said. "Just as those who obey our laws are welcome, those who break them must face the consequences."
Later in the day, Clinton was scheduled to meet the Mexican people in the historic colonial town centre of Tlaxcala, a small city 75 miles (120 km) east of Mexico City.
After a lunch with Zedillo in Tlaxcala, Clinton was to visit Mexico's famous pre-Columbian pyramids at Teotihuacan before returning to the capital for a quick visit to the U.S. embassy.
He was then to board Air Force One for a flight to Costa Rica, the next leg of his Latin America trip, where he will meet Central American leaders.
